subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce the appointment of Mr. George Vickers Haythorne as deputy minister of labour. Mr. Haythorne has held the position of assistant deputy minister after a very distinguished scholastic career at the University of Alberta and Harvard University, from which he received a Ph.D. degree in economics. In addition, he has received certain fellowships and scholarships. He has had practical experience as secretary of the Nova Scotia economic council in Halifax from 1938 to 1942, and he was associated with the national selective service, Department of Labour. He was director of the agriculture, forestry and fisheries branch, and director of the economics and research branch up until 1953 for a period of five years. Since that date he has been assistant deputy minister of labour. He is well known for the various articles he has written on matters of economics and political science.

Mr. Speaker, I have been asked to make a statement on loans for university dormitories and municipal sewage treatment projects. Last December the scope of the National Housing Act was broadened to include two entirely new concepts of federal government lending. Hon. members will recall that the amendments empowered Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with the approval of the governor in council to make long term, low interest loans to Canadian universities to assist in providing resident student accommodation, and to municipalities to aid in the construction or expansion of municipal sewage treatment projects.

maintopic: HARBOURS
subsubtopic: REPORTED DELAY IN LOADING RUS- SIAN GRAIN SHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had notice of a similar question from the hon. member for Vancouver East, and I think I will answer them both.
I am advised that loading the Russian ship Tiksi did consume a longer period of time than usual. Several factors contributed to this particular ship being in Vancouver 12 days in all. The Tiksi is a high, three-deck type of vessel not usually loaded with grain in Vancouver. Owing to its construction, the normal flow of grain was considerably reduced. The particular grades of wheat required to make up its full cargo of 10,345 tons necessitated a move from one elevator to another. A considerable portion of the grain had to be sacked, which is a time consuming operation. There were two other vessels taking grain at the berth where the Tiksi was completed, which left only two belts available for the Russian ship during this period. On one day, loading operations were suspended owing to a severe storm. The ship arrived in port during a busy week and was obliged to lay over a week end.
It is very unlikely that a similar situation will occur, and every effort is being made to give good service to shipping in Vancouver harbour.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, supplementary protocol No. 1 to the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, supplementary protocol No. 2 to the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, and the memorandum of understanding on the application of article XV of the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, all of which were signed in Paris on December 14, 1960; and that this house do approve the above agreements.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this convention is a most important one and marks a tremendous step forward in the economic field. We are happy today to have present in the gallery of this house Mr. Torkil Kristensen, secretary general designate of O.E.C.D. He is a leader in his native Denmark and one of our most respected allies in the field of economic cooperation in NATO. He is here for the purpose of acquainting members of the government with some of the features of this convention in so far as implementation is concerned and the terms thereof.
It is intended, by the establishment of O.E.C.D., to assist in the sustained economic growth and expansion of multilateral trade on a non-discriminatory basis, to the end that economic equilibrium will be secured which will constitute a major contribution not only to the strength and welfare of each and all the member nations, but to the assurance that the countries participating shall remain economically strong and shall have regard to the effect of the policies of each on other member nations. The task of reconstruction in western Europe is essentially complete. It is important at this time, however, that regard be had to supplementing and strengthening rather than replacing existing organizations, while at the same time assuring that current international economic and trade policies shall be carried into effect within the limitations I have mentioned.
This organization, when established, will not take the place of other organizations such as the general agreement on tariffs and trade or the international monetary fund, but will provide a high degree of consultation, close association and co-operation which should be effective instruments for broad and continuing co-operation. It is particularly important that there shall be maintained the closest

Economic Co-operation and Development consultation on all types of economic and financial policies, especially in connection with finding solutions to current international gold and foreign exchange reserve problems as well as in the other fields to which O.E.C.D. will apply.
The acceptance of this convention will recognize the growing interdependence of nations, and the fact that the better oil nations shall contribute to the growth and prosperity of the world community. What I intend to do is simply traverse in a general way something of the field of O.E.C.D., leaving it to the Minister of Finance to deal at length with such portions of the convention as he may deem appropriate. He has taken a large part in bringing about the adherence of Canada to this organization. He was present with the present Minister of Veterans Affairs at Paris in January, 1960 when the general framework of this organization was laid. In July, 1960 he went by himself to attend these meetings on behalf of the Canadian government and, finally, was present at the signing of the convention in December, 1960. At that time, he was accompanied by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure the house would expect me, as I most willingly do, to pay tribute particularly to the Minister of Finance for all he has done in order to enable the inclusion of Canada among the nations comprising this organization.
The convention provides for the establishment of the organization for economic cooperation and development and, as I said a moment ago, constitutes a great step forward for the countries of the Atlantic community. Indeed, it is no exaggeration to say that this is one of the most important agreements that have come before this house in recent years. One week ago yesterday I discussed this matter with President Kennedy in Washington, and I can say that he fully shares the view I have expressed as to the importance of this convention.
In order to grasp the significance of this development, one has to go back to the unprecedented offer of the United States in 1947 whereby the United States undertook to help European countries help themselves. The full extent of the material and social destruction wrought by war was only then becoming evident. In spite of large scale financial assistance already extended from both the United States and Canada, the European countries acting individually lacked the resources to import vitally needed food and new materials. On the political scene, the freedom and independence fought for at so great a cost seemed once again to be in serious jeopardy.
[Mr. DiefenbakerJ
European statesmen moved rapidly in response to the offer to draw up a joint European recovery program and established an organization, the organization for European economic co-operation, designed to allocate United States aid and promote European economic development. In 1950 both Canada and the United States became associated with this organization with the status of associated countries.
All who have visited Europe have seen something of the phenomenal recovery of the European countries. Indeed, this recovery has been one of the most significant achievements in this era since the war. The extraordinary economic growth and development of the European countries fully attests to the high degree of economic co-operation achieved among themselves and with their partners on this side of the Atlantic, and is a tribute to the industry and imagination of not only the leaders of the several countries concerned but their peoples as well. Indeed, when one looks at the developments since the war and the degree to which ancestral enemies in Europe have become trusted friends-one sees the relationship between France and Germany, enemies for a hundred years-one begins to appreciate that indeed in this age we have seen changes that few could have contemplated or even imagined.
The restoration of external convertibility of major European currencies marked the end of the post-war period, and has underlined the fact that Europe is again in a position to contribute her full share to the solution of the wider economic issues facing the free world.
The accompanying development of the last decade has been the creation of regional groupings, the E.E.C. or common market composed of France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg, and also the European free trade association composed of the United Kingdom, Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Portugal, Switzerland and Austria. The Canadian government has repeatedly emphasized its hope that these developments would not lead to any loss of traditional Canadian export markets in Europe; and while all the problems in this connection have not been solved, we believe that through close consultation with the European partners these problems will be solved and solved in a manner consistent with the maintenance of the growing interdependence among nations. We believe, and I think the house will agree, that a trade rift within Europe or between Europe and other western countries would be a matter of the greatest concern for all the free countries of the world.

Outside Europe there have also been rapid and significant developments, particularly in the less developed areas of the world. More and more we realize this tact, that there cannot be peace in the world with the peoples of the world half hungry or unpossessed of their minimum needs or lacking the opportunities of those of us who live in those parts of the world where the economies are strong and effective.
Many newly independent countries face the formidable task of raising the living standards of their peoples through economic development, they will not be able to do it by themselves. As the hon. member for Greenwood has so frequently said in this house, if we fail to realize their dependence on us we shall indeed reap a harvest in the years ahead which will not be in keeping with the opportunities that are ours. There is a challenge to the more prosperous countries to devise means, as the hon. gentleman has said so frequently in what I might describe as a crusade which he has undertaken, to encourage and assist those countries through aid and trade policies.
The decision to establish a new framework of economic co-operation including Canada and United States reflects the fact that the purely European goals of the O.E.E.C. has been largely realized. We now face the 1960's. If we are to meet the challenges of this decade I believe that the co-operating countries must forge new and stronger links with each other, and in the preparatory discussions in Paris there was recognition of the need of a new framework for co-operation which would reflect the needs of this decade. While the European economies are now prosperous and largely free of trade controls and restrictions, there are compelling reasons to reaffirm interdependence through concrete co-operation and to realize the fact, as I said earlier, that economic maladjustment whether in Europe or in North America is necessarily of common concern and importance to the western countries on either side of the Atlantic.
All these challenges that we face are well expressed in the three basic goals of the new organization. They are, to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living of member countries while maintaining financial stability and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy. Next, to contribute to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development; and finally, to contribute to the expansion in world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations.
Economic Co-operation and Development
The O.E.C.D. will not provide ready made solutions to these questions or a solution to the trade problems arising through the establishment of the two European regional economic groupings, but the historic significance of what is being done reflects the decision of the free countries on both sides of the north Atlantic to join together and co-operate closely in working out solutions to these problems for their own benefit and for the benefit of other countries throughout the world. The O.E.C.D. has value for Canada and is of special significance to Canada. It brings together countries of the Atlantic area, countries with which we have had historical, political, cultural and economic ties at a time when the traditional pattern of western economic and commercial relationships was undergoing profound and rapid changes. I think I can go further than that and say that I expect that in time other European countries will become associated in the co-operative work of the O.E.C.D.
I might digress for a moment and say something of the organization and of the protocols referred to in the resolution. The convention will come into effect following ratification. That is provided for in the agreement, which says that the convention will come into effect before the 30th September, 1961, upon the deposit of instruments of ratification or acceptance by all the signatories; or on the same date if by that date 15 signatories or more have deposited such instruments as regards those signatories; and after that date, but not later than two years from the signature of this convention, upon the deposit of such instruments by 15 signatories, as regards those signatories.
Some indication as to the comprehensiveness of the membership of the organization is shown by simply reading the list of countries participating: Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States of America. That is a comprehensive list of powers generally devoted to the preservation of individual liberty and the increase of general well-being.
The manner in which the objectives will be attained is contained in article 3, which reads as follows:
With a view to achieving the aims set out in article 1... the members agree that they will:
(a)	keep each other informed and furnish the organization with the information necessary for the accomplishment of its tasks;
(b)	consult together on a continuing basis, carry out studies and participate in agreed projects; and
(c)	co-operate closely and where appropriate take co-ordinated action.

Economic Co-operation and Development
There is also provision for aid to developing countries, which it is realized demands the support of all countries rather than being restricted to a few countries, as is often the case. The question as to the structure of the various committees will be dealt with by the Minister of Finance. There is, however, one committee to which I intend to make reference. That is the agriculture and fisheries committee, which is of particular interest to primary industries in Canada.
The provision respecting this economic field provides that there shall be consultations on agricultural, food and fishery policies with a view to promoting the harmonious development of these policies among member countries; that there shall be an examination of the over-all situation of agriculture and fisheries in member countries and of the prospects, including examination of the trend of supply and demand; studies of the possibilities for improving the marketing and distribution of these products with a view to determining measures which could be adopted nationally and internationally; surveys of the market situation for the main agricultural and fisheries products; and formulation in co-operation of proposals for remedial measures in the event of market difficulties; and generally assistance in the agricultural field to the economic, trade, and technical activities of the other bodies of the organization; the promotion of a better use of production factors and of technical progress in the sectors of agriculture and fisheries.
That is a most important section and one that has very great importance economically to Canada, as it has to other countries. The Minister of Finance will deal with the negotiations that took place and generally with the technical fields with which he has been so intimately connected.
I now wish to say a word with regard to the operation of O.E.C.D. in the economic field. I do not take this convention as one that will substitute action for the provisions of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, article II, with reference to economics. Article II reads as follows:
The parties will contribute towards the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free Institutions, by bringing about a better understanding on the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stabilization and well-being. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
I said this organization would not be a substitute for article II of NATO, but I believe that the nations comprising NATO, having failed to implement by action article II, have left for this organization a large field of economic collaboration. I also believe
that O.E.C.D. will carry out, in the main, the hopes of the nations which are signatories to the NATO agreement in the field of economic development, co-operation and collaboration.
This government contends that the organization will help to safeguard the vital trade interests of Canada and ensure that they will be fully taken into account by member countries as those member countries develop their respective policies. We expect that the activities of the new organization will supplement and reinforce the work of the other international arrangements, as I said earlier, including the United Nations specialized agencies.
The O.E.C.D. will require broad support, not only from governments but from the peoples of the member countries and, in particular, from both management and labour. Some consideration is being given to arrangements which would provide for some form of parliamentary association being set up in connection with the new organization which would serve to make the purposes and activities of the organization more widely known.
As one of those who advocated the setting up of the NATO parliamentary association, I believe that a similar body, not in the nature of one that recommends the adoption of policy but rather in the nature of an inquiring organization, would do much to increase the knowledge not only of the participating members of parliament belonging to such an organization but the Canadian people as a whole. My hope is that the O.E.C.D. will become an enduring association. It cannot do so unless there is on the part of all member countries a willingness to make their full contribution through co-operation and consultation in order to ensure the effective use of their respective capacities and potentialities.
I have read the debates of one of the parliamentary institutions of a nation that is giving consideration to this convention and I know that concern and fears have been expressed regarding some of its provisions. I do not share those fears or that concern. I believe that through the establishment of O.E.C.D. the countries of Europe and of North America will be serving notice of their right to co-operate among themselves and with others in order to attain the economic betterment of themselves and of all other nations.
I am seeking the approval of the house for this convention believing that its approval will mean that Canada will give full support to this organization. Our approval will constitute a declaration by Canadians that they intend to contribute to the best of their abilities and capacities to the achievement of its basic purposes.
I mentioned earlier that I discussed this organization with Mr. Kristensen. I was deeply

impressed by his dedication to its principles and his realization of the need for cooperation. Today there are signs, as there have been in the last several years, of some weakening in the NATO organization. The nations comprising the North Atlantic Treaty Organization must not permit that thing to take place for any weakening of the organization or of any of its member nations will inevitably lead to the danger of attack and will diminish the certainty of survival.
On the other hand, this organization has principles which are founded on co-operation in the economic field and, if its full implications are lived up to it will so strengthen the economies of each of the member nations as to assure the economic strength of all of us. Thereby it will make a contribution to the maintenance of peace not only among the member nations but throughout the world. I ask the house to give its support to this motion.
Canada since 1945 has demonstrated its belief in the basic principles upon which O.E.C.D. is founded. Canada believes that this organization will help to prevent the break-up of Europe into competitive trade groups or blocs, a potential danger that can only lead to a great and real danger in the future.
Canada also believes that O.E.C.D. will bring together not only the nations of NATO but also the members of the Six and the Seven and will foster good relations between Canada and the United States on the continent of North America in the economic field. While history shows that many of the wars that have taken place have been the consequence of economic competition, this organization is designed to remove the danger of that possibility and to bring about a new unity among nations whose economic strength, when exercised in unity with full respect for the sovereignty of the member nations, can assure that mankind itself and people everywhere will see new economic vistas achieved in their time and generation and thereby the removal of a major cause of potential war. I ask the house to give support to this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minisier of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the light of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) I shall be glad now to take the opportunity to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and of enlarging upon some of the aspects of the organization for economic co-operation and development which have been the subject of the Prime Minister's remarks.
On previous occasions I have reported to the house in some detail on the steps taken over the past 13 months which led to the signing of the O.E.C.D. convention by ministers of the 20 countries concerned in Paris in December. I do not propose to review this ground further. The statements are to be found in Hansard of last session.
I should like to say, however, that the successful conclusion of these negotiations in a relatively brief period of time was a significant achievement. It could not have been accomplished without sustained and devoted effort by all those concerned. The representatives of all countries approached the difficult task of reconstituting the O.E.E.C. in a spirit of co-operation that augurs well for the future success of the organization. With this spirit and sense of purpose, I have every confidence that the O.E.C.D. will realize the high aims to which it is committed.
What are these aims? Briefly stated, they are threefold: first, to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth in member countries while maintaining financial stability and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy; second, to contribute to the economic development of less developed countries by increasing and improving the flow of capital and technical assistance; third, to promote the expansion of world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis.
The first of these aims is fundamental. The other two cannot be achieved if the first is not achieved. Sustained economic growth including high levels of employment of resources, monetary stability and equilibrium in international payments are major objectives of economic policy in all countries. If we in the western industrial countries are to achieve a more abundant life in freedom, both for ourselves and for the newly developing areas in the world, we must grow. On such growth depends our ability to raise our own living standards, to give assistance to others and to provide markets for the fruitful expansion of international trade.
The desirability of strong and vigorous growth is self-evident. What perhaps is not so apparent is that it has become increasingly difficult to achieve such growth by unilateral action. Progress made in liberalization of
2496	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development trade and payments since the war and the introduction of convertibility of the major European currencies in the last two years have led to a growing interdependence of the various national economies. They have become more sensitive to changes in world trends and to measures taken in other countries. There are now important limitations on the action which individual countries can allow themselves to take without regard to the external repercussions of their decisions. There are also limitations on the effectiveness of action that any individual country may take in isolation. The program just announced by the President of the United States for improving the United States balance of payments provides a striking illustration of this interdependence. The success of this program will depend to a considerable degree on the extent to which the major western European countries pursue compatible policies. There is thus a clear need for co-operation in economic policy if we are to experience sustained and growing prosperity without sacrificing financial stability.
It is in this context that the O.E.C.D. is likely to prove particularly valuable. It will provide a forum for regular and continuing consultation and review of the economic and financial situation in member countries and the policies pursued by member governments. Special attention will be paid to the international effects of national policies. For this purpose the O.E.C.D. will have two committees, namely the economic policy committee and the economic and development review committee. The economic policy committee will keep under review the economic and financial situation of member countries with a view to attaining the objectives of the convention. It is intended that its sessions be attended by senior officials from national capitals who are intimately familiar with the formulation of economic policies in their own countries. Canada participated in a similar committee in the O.E.E.C. and found it valuable. We believe it will be increasingly useful in the years ahead and that those consultations and discussions will prove to be the central part of the activities of the new organization. If these consultations are to be fruitful, members must have clear knowledge of the problems faced by one another and the techniques used to deal with them. Accordingly, it has been decided to establish an economic and development review committee to hold annual detailed examinations of the economic situation of member countries. In this committee member states will obtain the raw material, so to speak, as well as the understanding required for effective consultation about broad policies.


The O.E.C.D. will also have an important role to play in contributing to the expansion of the economies of the less developed countries. The vast majority of the world's peoples live under the bondage of a grinding poverty from which they are determined to free themselves. The extent to which they succeed may well prove vital to the future peace and well-being of all mankind. If the free industrialized countries are to be true to the highest values of their civilization, as well as to their own economic and political interests, they must assist in this great endeavour.
Their acceptance of this responsibility has already been demonstrated by their participation in the economic assistance program of the United Nations, the international bank for reconstruction and development, the international finance corporation and the international development association as well as through programs such as the Colombo plan. Let me emphasize that the O.E.C.D. will not in any sense replace or weaken these existing agencies and programs. Its main function in the field of aid will be to provide an informal forum in which aid programs and policies can be discussed frankly and be made more effective. In this way we hope it will stimulate an increased flow of aid to developing areas as well as help to ensure that existing resources are used more effectively. It will not, however, establish and administer aid programs of its own. It will not limit or change the nature of Canada's existing programs, such as the Colombo plan, nor will it involve any Canadian obligation to provide additional assistance.
The main body for consultations on aid programs will be the development assistance committee, sometimes called DAG. This committee will take over the functions and characteristics of the development assistance group which was formed early in 1960, and which has already had three meetings.
The development assistance committee will be concerned with methods of providing assistance to non-member countries. The problems of the less developed member countries will be the concern of two other subsidiary bodies. The O.E.E.C. is already engaged in useful programs of technical assistance in less developed member countries, particularly Greece and Turkey. It is expected that these programs will be continued under the aegis of the technical assistance committee. In addition, the development programs of members in the process of development will be discussed in the economic and development review committee.
The extent to which the O.E.C.D. will succeed in stimulating economic growth and in providing increased assistance to developing

areas will depend to a significant degree on the maintenance and continued vigorous growth of international trade. This fact is recognized in the organization's third major aim, which is to contribute to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations. The words "in accordance with international obligations" make it clear that membership in the O.E.C.D. in no way subtracts from the obligations which participating countries have assumed through their adherence to GATT and their membership in the international monetary fund. The purpose of discussions in the O.E.C.D. will be to strengthen the effectiveness of these more broadly based institutions and to promote the fulfilment of their objectives. I think it important to stress the nature of this relationship for two reasons. First, it is only by supporting the authority of GATT and the I.M.F. and collaborating with them that the O.E.C.D. will be able to realize its aims in the field of trade and payments. Second, I should like to allay any apprehensions among non-participating countries that the industrial countries of Europe and North America intend to concentrate on their own affairs at the expense of other countries.
From what I have said it follows that the organization's function in the field of trade will be essentially consultative. It has been agreed that much of the earlier activity of the O.E.E.C. in the field of trade, which was based upon a regional approach to European reconstruction, is no longer appropriate and will be discontinued. It is not intended that O.E.C.D. will establish or administer new trade rules. The proposed trade committee will be used for frank discussions of general trade policies and practices, for the examination of specific trade problems primarily of interest to members and their overseas territories and for the consideration of any outstanding short and long term problems between the six countries of the European economic community and the seven countries of the European free trade area association. Within these terms of reference it is hoped that any member country may obtain prompt consideration and discussion by the trade committee of trade measures by another member which may adversely affect its interest, with a view to removing or minimizing such adverse effects. In establishing these terms of reference account has been taken of the interests of outside countries and arrangements will be made for attendance of representatives of the GATT at meetings of the trade committee.
One task of the trade committee may be to consider the problems created by the formation of the two regional trading groups
Economic Co-operation and Development in western Europe. Some work has already been done in this field by the committee on trade problems which was set up on a temporary basis at the Paris meetings in January, I960. Its work will be taken over by the O.E.C.D. Canada clearly has an important interest in the policies of these two groups and in the nature of any accommodation which may ultimately be reached between them.
The broad activities I have mentioned in the fields of economic policy consultations, aid and trade will be the main preoccupations of the new organization. In addition there will be a series of committees to handle work in more specific fields. There will be an agriculture committee, whose work we hope will be closely integrated with that of other bodies within the organization, to consider agricultural problems and policies pertinent to the organization's objectives. A similar committee will be established to deal with fisheries problems. The organization will also have subsidiary bodies with responsibilities in the field of science and technology. Their task will be to stimulate member countries to increase and to use more efficiently their scientific manpower, and their training and research facilities. The organization is expected to fulfil this role by acting as a clearing house for information and experience and by means of consultations, conferences and the provision of fellowships.
Provision has also been made for co-operation among member states in a number of other fields including tourism, manpower, maritime transport, energy and industry. The European nuclear energy agency, in which members of the O.E.E.C. co-operated in the development of the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, will be retained in its present form. Canada and the United States are to retain their present status as associate members. The European productivity agency of the O.E.E.C. is to be dissolved. Its responsibilities in the fields of science and technical assistance will be transferred to other bodies. Decisions with respect to the continuance of other activities of the E.P.A. will be taken during the coming year.
This then, Mr. Speaker, is an outline of the work on which the O.E.C.D. proposes to engage. I should like to turn now to the provisions of the convention which set forth how the organization is to govern itself in carrying out its manifold tasks.
A council composed of all members will be the supreme body, meeting either at the level of ministers or of permanent representatives. It is authorized to establish an executive committee and such other subsidiary bodies as may be required for the achievement of the organization's aims. There will be an
2498	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development international secretariat headed by a secretary general. He has been given considerable powers and authority. He will serve as chairman of the council when it meets at the level of permanent representatives and he may submit proposals to council or to any other body of the organization. He will be responsible only to council. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has told the house today, Professor Torkil Kristensen of Denmark has been selected to fill this extremely important post. Professor Kristensen is a former finance minister of Denmark and has a very distinguished political and administrative background.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
He has already proved his mettle as chairman of the O.E.C.D. preparatory committee which he guided through the arduous and complicated negotiations which preceded signature of the convention. It has been a great joy to the government and all others who have been conferring with Professor Kristensen and his colleagues during the past two days that it has been possible for him and them to pay this present visit to Canada.
To achieve its aims the organization may take decisions binding on all members and make recommendations to members. It will not be able to do so, however, without unanimous agreement. In other words, each member has the power of veto. A member may abstain from voting on a particular decision or recommendation and if it does so that decision or recommendation will not apply to it. It is clear therefore that the organization cannot take action respecting a member without the consent of that member.
There will doubtless be some situations in which it would be desirable for the organization to use its power of decision and recommendation. At the same time I believe it would be wise to do so sparingly. To achieve its major objectives it must rely on action on the part of the individual governments. Governments are more likely to be influenced through the process of discussion itself, in the economic policy committee and other committees, than through the mere formality of a council decision or recommendation.
The last provision of the convention which I should like to discuss is article 15 and the related memorandum of understanding on its application. Under the provisions of this article all acts of the O.E.E.C. council, including decisions, recommendations and resolutions, will lapse, except those which the council of the successor organization decides to carry over. The acts of the O.E.E.C. were


examined in the O.E.C.D. preparatory committee in order to determine which should be recommended for retention by the O.E.C.D. with modifications, where necessary, in order to adapt them to the functions of the new organization. Several member countries wished to have reasonable assurance that the recommendations of the preparatory committee would in fact be endorsed by the O.E.C.D. council. A memorandum of understanding to ensure this result was drawn up at their request.

speechtext:
Attendance was chiefly in the hands of Mr. Peter Towe. Mr. Jules Leger was, of course, associated with the representation of Canada in this regard until his illness, and following his illness he was very capably represented by Mr. Peter Towe. Having had some opportunity myself of observing the quality of the work done by Mr. Peter Towe in representing Canada at Paris in this regard, it gives me much pleasure to pay tribute to the excellence of the work he performed.
I said that a memorandum of understanding to ensure what I have referred to as an assurance that the recommendations of the preparatory committee would in fact be endorsed by the O.E.C.D. council was drawn up at the request of several countries. Under it members of the O.E.E.C. are committed to voting for the recommendations of the preparatory committee when these are considered for approval in the O.E.C.D. council. However, Canada and the United States, which are not full members of the O.E.E.C., have been permitted a certain latitude in this respect. We will be released from voting for any recommended act which we specify in a notice to the preparatory committee not later than ten days after the deposit of our instrument of ratification of the convention.
Not all the acts which the preparatory committee has recommended for retention will apply to Canada. Some of them contain provisions which conflict with Canadian legislation or practice. In these cases we have stated that we either would not adhere or would adhere only with specific reservations. Most of the acts which will apply to us are decisions of a technical nature or are relatively unimportant recommendations which are not binding, but merely have to be taken into consideration, thus leaving leaving participat-

ing countries freedom of judgment as to the action that may be required. The review of the acts is not yet complete.
The convention I have described, Mr. Speaker, is a flexible instrument. It is designed to equip each of its members better for the challenging roles which await us. Just as in the past 12 years solutions were found through the O.E.E.C. to many problems confronting western Europe, so in the future 18 nations in Europe and two on the western side of the north Atlantic will seek solutions to their common problems through the O.E.C.D.
In the O.E.C.D. Canada and the other members have attested their mutual interest, their common purpose, their interdependence and the renewed vigour with which we shall pursue our declared economic goals. In all aspects of our work we shall be mindful of our responsibilities throughout the world.
To a greater extent than perhaps has ever been the case we live in one world. That world is full of dangers and difficulties. But it also holds great promise of a life in which we can realize our full potential as individuals and as part of the human family. It is my firm belief that through the O.E.C.D. we can move toward this great ideal, that this organization can effectively serve the high hopes of the free world and that it can contribute to the prosperity and well-being of our own people and of other peoples throughout the world. With the willingness of member states to use their capacities and potentialities to promote the objectives of O.E.C.D., I believe the new organization will prove to be a major step forward in international economic co-operation. The Canadian government will do all that lies within its power to ensure that this potential is realized.
The convention has been submitted to the congress of the United States for approval, and is under debate. I believe it has not yet been submitted to the parliament of any other member country of the O.E.C.D. which signed the convention in Paris in December last. Thus, Mr. Speaker, is given to the Canadian parliament the honour, if it so chooses, of being the first parliament among the parliaments of the 20 member countries of O.E.C.D. to give approval to the convention and thus to lead the way to what we believe is a bright future for a beneficent international institution.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution
which is before the house, as has been said, is an important one. It deals with extremely important questions and asks the house to approve the setting up of what may become a very important institution. I can say at
Economic Co-operation and Development once, Mr. Speaker, that so far as the official opposition is concerned we are happy to approve the resolution. We wish the institution well, and we hope it will accomplish what it is designed to accomplish in the convention establishing it, which has been signed by a representative of the Canadian government and which is now up for approval.
The importance of this resolution lies not only in its terms, in the convention which sets up the organization for economic cooperation and development, but also in the implications of the organization itself and of the approval that we are being asked to give to the convention setting it up. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has pointed out this afternoon this convention, in a sense, marks the culmination of the work of European reconstruction. We are honoured, as has been said already, in having in the gallery this afternoon one of those dedicated Europeans who has done so much to bring about not only the successful completion of the work leading up to this convention but all the progressive steps that have been taken toward European unity.
In this organization referred to in the convention we now have a new and broader framework not only for European economic co-operation but for Atlantic economic cooperation. The organization which we are being asked to approve, through approval of the convention, replaces the organization for European economic co-operation which in its day has been invaluable in aiding the progress of Europe toward economic co-operation and unity. I should like to pay my tribute to the work of O.E.E.C., which was so important and with which Canada and the United States have been associated. In replacing O.E.E.C., with Canada as an observer, we are being asked now to approve the full membership of Canada in this new broader organization along with the membership of the United States. I think the extension of membership in that way is not only important but is gratifying.
The Prime Minister said that the organization for economic co-operation and development is not meant to replace in any way article 2 of NATO. I think I am reporting his words accurately. We in this house should not wish, I am sure, to take any action which would weaken NATO in any degree as an organization for collective defence. If anything should be done in that direction, it should be to strengthen NATO. I am not sure, however-and only events will show this-whether the new organization will [DOT] not in fact begin to replace the work of economic co-operation which was visualized as being performed by NATO under article 2, but concerning which there have always been great
2500	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development difficulties in implementation, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) knows so well.
Indeed, I think I am right in saying that in a discussion before the Senate foreign relations committee of the United States the secretary of the treasury indicated that this organization may eventually take over a great deal, if not all of the work, that it had been hoped might have been done by the implementation of article 2 of NATO. The secretary of the treasury, Mr. Dillon, himself did a great deal to bring the negotiations on O.E.C.D. to a successful conclusion when he was the assistant secretary of state. However, I do not believe we need to worry too much about this possibility provided that such a development did not interfere with other aspects of NATO in any way, shape or form. After all, O.E.C.D. does provide an enlarged foundation at least for Atlantic economic cooperation because when it comes into existence it will include several countries that are not now members of NATO, and their absence from NATO was one of the reasons it was so difficult to use that organization as an agency for economic co-operation.
O.E.C.D. not only has two North American members of NATO in its proposed membership, but I believe I am right in saying every European country except those behind the iron curtain. The minister will correct me if I am wrong.

speechtext: And Spain.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS

No, I think Spain is a member of O.E.C.D. I believe, therefore, there is at least the broadest possible foundation for Atlantic economic co-operation and development in this organization. It will be interesting to see the action and interaction between the economic discussions of the existing NATO organization under article 2 and the development of O.E.C.D. Although none of the expressions that have been used today by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance give us any reason to believe that they have this matter in mind in asking us to approve this convention, perhaps this organization with its broad membership may become an effective foundation for Atlantic development, and not only in the field of economic consultation.
One who has had a good deal to do with these matters, namely Lord Gladwyn, whom we perhaps know better as Sir Gladwyn Jebb, speaking in the House of Lords on January 20 of this year, had this to say when he was dealing with European co-operation and development, and the desirability of NATO as an agency for that purpose:
My Lords, such a body exists. It is true that, for political reasons, it cannot call itself an Atlantic community, but that, in effect, is what it is. I refer, of course, to O.E.C.D.-the Organization


for Economic Co-operation and Development-the 20 members of which comprise all non-communist European states this side of the iron curtain save Finland, plus the United States and Canada.
It does not at present represent a unity-some of its members are members of military alliances, and some most emphatically, are not-but it does represent a common, and basically Christian, tradition, an ethnic affiliation, a geographical area and an economically homogeneous group. Australia and New Zealand are the only really similar countries in the world which are not included, and they, after all, are situated many thousands of miles away from the Atlantic. Six of the members of O.E.C.D. are already on the way to becoming unified. Others may (and, personally, I hope they will) join that unity. But that will not harm O.E.C.D.-rather the reverse.
Eventually, I hope, it will become rather more coherent. Some day, no doubt, with the aid of those excellent NATO parliamentarians, I trust it will develop an assembly of its own. At this point it might well even absorb the council of Europe. But all this is for the future. At this moment, the rather anonymous Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development is as near a thing to an Atlantic community as we can achieve.
That is a vision for the future, but it is one to which I think most of us will subscribe as something which should be and one day I hope will be realized.
A much more limited expression of the significance of this organization-and I am not quarrelling with that expression-has been given to the house this afternoon by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance. Indeed, the minister himself referred to statements he made in earlier days of this session. They appear at page 196 of Hansard. He emphasized then and has repeated this afternoon that this organization is not meant in any way to override or replace GATT, and that larger trade questions and tariff matters will continue to be discussed within the ambit not of this organization but of GATT itself.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can welcome the expansion of the O.E.E.C. into the O.E.C.D. because it brings the United States and Canada into organic and full association as members of this new organization. The expansion is desirable but of course those who could follow the negotiations leading up to the signature, in so far as one can follow them in the press, know that this expansion was secured at a price. The price is in a sense the watering down, in some respects at least, of the commitments of the narrower and more limited organization of O.E.E.C. At an early stage in the negotiations I understand there was some difference in opinion as to whether trade should be even mentioned in the convention. Agreement was reached in that regard and trade fortunately is mentioned as a subject for consultation. But article 6, to which the Minister of Finance has referred limits the application of any recommendation or any decision taken by O.E.C.D. in trade or

in any other matter within the convention to those members of the organization who agree with the decision. In other words, every member of the organization has a veto in so far as that member is concerned over the application of any decision or recommendation.
I know that in all these matters the pursuit of perfection can sometimes lead to failure to achieve anything and it would perhaps have been quite impossible to secure any other result at this time in the negotiations on this subject of international economic co-operation. However, it is hoped that one day the practices of the O.E.E.C. may be acceptable to the members of this wider organization. As the minister has pointed out, that organization does provide for consultation, and that fact in itself can be important. It does not provide for much more than consultation in this field of trade policy and, more important, any consultation will depend on leadership and direction given by the governments inside this organization; I refer to leadership in the right direction which must be an extension of European movement toward economic co-operation and unity across the Atlantic. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that consideration will be the ultimate justification for this organization; namely its ability to make progress in that direction. No hope, of course, has been expressed today which would justify the feeling that this is going to be an easy or quick achievement.
When the O.E.C.D. was signed last December the press communique announcing the signature had this to say on the subject of trade:
In the field of trade the O.E.C.D. will carry out the following functions:	Confrontation on
general trade policies and practices at regular intervals or when requested by a member; examination of specific trade problems primarily of interest to members; and consideration of any outstanding short and long term problems falling within the terms of reference of the committee on trade problems established in January 1960.
The Minister of Finance in his statement in this house on December 16 to which I have already referred elaborated on the trade question in these words which I am quoting from page 866 of Hansard:
The organization will provide a continuing forum for consideration of the effect, on member countries and on others, of the trade groupings that are emerging in Europe. I refer of course, to issues arising from the formation of the Six and the Seven.
Then further down:
The new organization is, as I have said, to promote the expansion of trade on a multilateral and non-discriminatory basis, thus contributing to the achievement of the purposes of the general agreement on tariff and trade.
Mr. Speaker, in the statements we have had this afternoon from the Prime Minister
Economic Co-operation and Development and the Minister of Finance no light has been thrown on the attitude of the government towards these issues referred to by the minister on December 16th arising from the formation of the Six and the Seven. What we should like to hear, as perhaps we shall before this debate is over because it has a very direct relationship to O.E.C.D., is something about the attitude of the government toward the common market and European free trade area, and especially about how Canada's foreign economic policy is to be developed. Now that we are contemplating full partnership in this Atlantic organization we shall have even more to take into account the emergence of these new trade blocs, all the members of which will also be members of the organization for European Economic Cooperation and Development. The government, aside from certain statements, which have been interpreted as threats of retaliation, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) in Paris, and implied in some statements of the Minister of Finance.

Apart from these statements, Mr. Speaker, the government has given no indication of how it intends to meet the challenge or the opportunities presented by the development of the Six and the Seven. Perhaps there will be greater opportunity to deal with this matter now that Canada is a full member of the organization for economic cooperation and development. We have had no indication this afternoon as yet as to how the government will use Canadian membership in this proposed organization to promote Canadian economic interests, or in what direction Canada will use its influence in the furtherance of long-run economic objectives or in helping to solve these specific problems of the common market Six and the European free trade area with its Seven.
Surely information on that point is of importance before we approve of this particular resolution. Surely a solution of this problem, namely the relationship of the Six and the Seven within O.E.C.D., is of paramount importance to O.E.C.D. itself as it begins its operation. Together the European economic community, the common market, and the European free trade area make up 40 per cent-and we sometimes forget this fact-of world trade and the manner in which their trade relations develop will have a profound effect on the world in general
2502	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development and on Canada, I suggest, in particular. I hope to show this effect a little later.
The common market is now a growing concern. It is no longer any Utopian dream. Commenting not long ago on its first two years of operation the president of the commission of the European economic community, Professor Hallstein, made these claims for the common market. He said that the community is the world's second largest industrial power, and the world's largest trader; that its exports and imports have risen, as indeed they have risen in a most exciting way during its brief existence, resulting from-and we had better not forget this fact-the removal of trade barriers between the members of the common market. Professor Hallstein said that investment in 1959 in the common market countries had tripled in comparison with 1958. He also indicated that businessmen and industrialists inside the common market countries were now pressing for a speeding of the transition period, which I think is to extend over 15 years.
This glowing account, by a man who had so much to do with the formation and development of the common market, of a new and dynamic trading area of 165 million inhabitants is just one more evidence of the magnificent post-war recovery of western Europe. It is an example of what the removal of trade barriers can do in the promotion of economic prosperity. But in Canadian, and indeed in American minds it has also aroused a good deal of apprehension over the impact of a development of this kind on our trade with the common market and the free trade area countries which, as they develop, might take the wrong course. I will explain what I mean by that in a moment.
Perhaps this is one of the things in which the proposed organization we are discussing today can exercise an important and beneficial influence. I am referring to this apprehension which is felt in Canada as to the effect that these developments in Europe, if they take the wrong course, may have on jobs, income and trade. That apprehension was expressed not long ago before the Senate committee on manpower by the president of the Canadian exporters association when he asserted that the formation of the European trade bloc presents a grave situation for Canadian exporters into the area because of proposed high protective tariffs; that is, a high common tariff against non-members of the common market.
That apprehension is understandable because we know how important this market is to Canadian exporters. Indeed, at the present


time it is the third largest market for Canadian products. About 40 per cent of our sales to this market are in agricultural products, and another 40 per cent are in primary and semi-processed materials exported largely by the chemical, metal, mineral and pulp and paper industries. This European common market is now growing by leaps and bounds and it is of vital importance that not only should our products not be excluded from it as that growth takes place, because of a high external tariff but that we should be able to share in the advance being made by these European countries. I think that hope and that apprehension lie at the basis of our approach to this particular problem.
So we are bound to ask ourselves this question: will the common market create trade, or will it merely divert trade? Also we are bound to ask ourselves: can the O.E.C.D. in its operations exercise the kind of influence which will ensure the former, namely the expansion and creation of trade rather than the latter, namely merely the diversion of trade?
Naturally if the common market develops on the basis of increased protectionism against traders outside its membership, that would certainly divert the flow of trade rather than create new trade through specialization. The apprehension based on those dangers has been created from two sources. One is the averaging method used in setting the common market tariff against the rest of the world, and the range of commodities for which duties are fixed by negotiation.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-9, to incorporate International Brain Research Organization.
He said: Perhaps in introducing this bill, Mr. Speaker, I should offer a fairly comprehensive explanation concerning the establishment of this organization.
The purpose behind the organization is, I believe, well explained in the preamble to the statutes and bylaws. The preamble reads as follows:
Whereas there is need, throughout the world, for the mobilization and direction of a larger proportion of our best scientific resources for research on the brain, an international organization has been created for this purpose.
Progress in medicine generally has been great and in the physical sciences it has been even greater. We have witnessed the development of the atom bomb and the highly technical automated machinery of the last few decades. These developments have far outstripped our understanding of even the most elementary brain mechanisms upon which this fantastic progress is based.
All the achievements of man, including cultural and intellectual thought and behaviour in relation to social and physical environment and man's mental and physical health and welfare depend to a large measure on the relatively unexplored universe of the brain.
This has in the past and will in the future pose a most difficult problem to those who are devoting a great deal of their time and energy in an attempt to explore the universe of the brain and to devise methods of further exploring this realm. The methods and principles applied to the physical and biological sciences should be applied to research on the brain. Even the money applied to the physical sciences, for instance in the development of the atom bomb, far outstrips that which is being spent on research on the brain and the amount of creative energy devoted to the former exceeds that devoted to the latter.
The problems encountered in this field are of the greatest difficulty and complexity and are becoming increasingly acute. In psychiatry the revolution caused by the discovery of psychopharmacological agents and the recognition of the importance of basic knowledge of brain chemistry underlying mental disorder and behaviour, has brought into clear relief not only the importance of basic scientific work in this field, but also the depth and extent of our ignorance.
Within the last five years a revolution has occurred through the discovery of the action of certain psychopharmacological agents on the brain in terms of emulating the symptoms

of the mental disorder known as schizophrenia. In neurology there are many debilitating diseases of which we have no real understanding and for which we have no therapy. We feel that a more promising approach to some of the problems in neurology can be made through basic scientific work and biological work on fundamental mechanisms to determine the development of the brain and its function.
In communications, engineering and electronic computers, the need for more basic knowledge concerning how the brain perceives the outside world, how it records memories and how it solves problems, is becoming more acute.
In relation to jet space travel there is a tremendous amount of research required to get the basic knowledge of the brain's reaction to such travel. In brain research we have been very concerned with precise information about the organization and very fine structure of the brain, how it reacts to different biochemicals and how it reacts physiologically to changes in its environment.
In the realm of neurophysiology, with the development of the electronic microscope, we have been able to discover the reaction of single brain cells to stimuli, such as learning, fright, and so on. This is a tremendously difficult problem and very complex. I can recall -it is too long ago to admit to-before world war II, assisting as an interne in brain operations. Since world war II I have observed brain operations in one of the leading neurological hospitals in the western world, that in Montreal, and I can tell the house frankly that there has been terrific progress in brain study and operative technique in a matter of 25 or 26 years. I feel that this progress has been due to the work of those very selfless, devoted people in the brain research field who have not the backing that they should have, because of the lack of co-ordination between groups in different countries of the world which are doing research on brain diseases and functions of the brain. Although they have developed techniques and knowledge in those different centres, heretofore there has been no close collaboration between the findings and the knowledge of those different centres. It is hoped that with the setting up of this International Brain Research Organization greater facilities for coordination on an international scale will be brought about. This is to increase and accelerate the exchange of information and ideas between scientists of different countries.
The organization itself stems from a resolution passed by a number of brain research scientists in Moscow at an international meeting of neurologists in 1958. I hope no one will entertain any serious thoughts over the fact
Private Bills
that the birth of this organization got its stimulus in Moscow. It has no such appellation. The proposal to form this international brain research organization was then presented to the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization by this committee; that is, UNESCO. The first committee was headed by Professor H. Jasper of Montreal. At its tenth session, the general conference of UNESCO recommended that its responsibilities in the field of natural sciences be also extended to brain research. At a meeting in Paris in October, 1959, a study group formulated the main outlines of the organization. They also elected compilers to draw up lists of scientists to serve on seven international panels. These panels are really parts of the study of the brain and consist of the following:	neuroanatomy,
neurochemistry, neuroendocrinology, neuropharmacology, neurophysiology, behavioural sciences, neurocommunications and biophysics.
The council for the international organization of medical sciences was then charged by UNESCO with the task of helping in setting up the organization to be known as IBRO. Thus, in this bill we have the final act in the setting up of this international organization on brain research.
Over 250 scientists in more than 30 different countries were approached and asked whether they approved of the proposal, and if they did, to elect by ballot those of their scientists whom they wanted to represent them on the various panels. Then, those were to meet as delegates on a central committee held in October, 1960 in Paris.
By July of 1960 an overwhelming majority of the panel members gave their consent in writing and elected their representatives to this central committee, and IBRO was then definitely established. What of this organization? One of its main functions, certainly at the beginning, will be to foster knowledge between different panels of the different countries throughout the world.
As hon. members can readily understand, the research scientists in brain work in Moscow had little liaison, for instance, with the brain research scientists in the United States of America. By means of this organization, which is to be set up with headquarters in Montreal, the findings of those panels or disciplines in the U.S.S.R. will be centralized and funnelled through the central headquarters in Montreal and will be made available not only to scientists in the U.S.S.R. but to brain scientists all over the world. Not only in information alone will this procedure prove of great value to those countries which are just developing and have not as yet research facilities, but this information will be provided in their own language through making

Private Bills
use of the facilities of UNESCO for translator! and compilation for the IBRO. They also hope through their program of action to set up fellowships and provide for the exchange of scientific workers. Strangely enough, in the scientific world national and cultural lines do not seem to make very much difference, and the exchange of workers is felt to be of a great deal of importance in this organization. They also think they will be able to provide the facilities and the money to set up temporary research teams.
Through their teaching facilities they also hope to promote world-wide education with regard to brain research. I must say that any research work is a very thankless task. Such workers are not too highly paid. The work takes a great deal of time and effort and even considerable loss of sleep in order to reach an objective. Many who have struggled for years on a project have not yet reached their objective.
They also hope, particularly in the underdeveloped countries, to help in the extension of existing laboratory facilities. Finally, by means of international meetings and conferences which will be held at least every two years they hope to exchange information and to extend their knowledge to research groups throughout the world. I hope the bill will pass without any amendment.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN GENERAL COUNCIL OF THE BOY SCOUTS ASSOCIATION
THE CANADIAN GENERAL COUNCIL OF THE BOY SCOUTS ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-ll, respecting the Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is essentially very simple. It is to change the name of the Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association, in English, to Boy Scouts of Canada or, in French, Scouts du Canada. Although this appears to be a very simple thing and perhaps would require little explanation, there is a greater significance to this change in view of what has been happening in the boy scout movement in Canada during the years since the last war.
If one looks at the explanatory note, one will find that the present name, the Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association, was established when this association was, in effect, a branch of the Boy Scouts Association incorporated by royal charter in London, England, in 1912, Since that time the Canadian boy scout movement has become an

Private Bills
independent body within the international boy scouts conference. The retention of the old name could lead to contradictions and misunderstandings as it does not indicate the independence of the Canadian body.
I think that this is a particularly appropriate year for this action to be taken because on January 27 the boy scouts headquarters moved into its new building in Ottawa which had been long dreamed of, long planned for and worked toward. This building will enable the association to conduct its affairs with even greater efficiency than in the past and also enable it to expand the services which a membership in Canada of approximately 300,000 now requires. It is a rather interesting statistic that in Canada today, a relatively small nation in population, there are 300,000 boy scouts, wolf cubs and their voluntary leaders. This number is growing rapidly. I think it is interesting also to note that in July of this year 3,500 boy scouts from all parts of Canada will be in Ottawa to take part in the Canadian jamboree. There will be in attendance representatives of the Boy Scouts of America, and probably some from Mexico and the other countries of the Americas.
In referring to this matter of the growth of the organization, I would place particular emphasis on the Canadianization of the organization, although I do not do so in any narrow nationalistic sense. It is appropriate, I believe, to consider exactly the place that scouting is taking in the lives of the people all across Canada. I think it is interesting to realize that the movement is now about 50 years old in Canada. As a matter of fact, scouts and wolf cubs are so familiar to us in all our communities that we pretty much take them for granted. We perhaps overlook the fact that this large organization could not continue to exist unless it had the sympathy, understanding and co-operation of individual citizens in every community in which it was established.
A portion of the funds of the association is earned by the boy scouts and wolf cubs through their various ventures and a substantial proportion is obtained from individual citizen subscriptions. Without this assistance the movement could not continue.
We have several thousand men and women acting as voluntary leaders and devoting many hundreds of hours during the year to the training of these boy scouts and wolf cubs. We should realize that this association with its national, provincial, district and city headquarters at various places throughout the country is maintaining a high standard of training for the youth of this country. We should realize that the training standards are jealously guarded by the Canadian association. Training programs for leaders have become widespread and a

greater number of adults each year are spending their spare time in an effort to maintain the standard at this high level. I feel it is also important to realize that this effort will only be successful if the people engaged in public life take the time to examine the standards, aims and objectives of organizations such as the Boy Scouts Association. I feel that private citizens should also consider the contribution they can make toward the continued successful operation of this valuable movement.
Boy scout and wolf cub groups exist in every province and in every territory in Canada. Many of the members of this organi-ation have distinguished themselves over the years in many fields. The boy scout movement is essentially an international organization of brotherhood which has as an objective the developing of self-reliance. But during times of war former boy scouts have served well and I am sure the younger boys will continue to do so.
I feel that the underlying significance of this move to change the name is an effort to emphasize a program that has been accelerated during the years since the war. This effort has been fostered by a sense of Cana-dianism in regard to the scout program. There has been no departure from the principles of scouting as laid down by Lord Baden Powell in 1908. The objectives vary in different areas and here in Canada we must keep in mind the geographic and climatic conditions of our country. There is in existence, a program an object of which is to promote out-of-doors activities during 12 months of the year. Only a few years ago, I was somewhat surprised when I found myself learning how to camp under canvas in the mountains of British Columbia in January. I felt that this was a marvellous objective for young boys. I was not too sure that it was a marvellous thing for myself. In any event it is as a result of the efforts of the leaders that this program is continuing in a way that provides leadership and training for Canadian youth.
All of the things I have mentioned justify our attention and support. I believe that the change in name as suggested at this time emphasizes to the members of the movement as well as to the public in general that the boy scouts of Canada are endeavouring to contribute to those things we in Canada like to regard as distinctively Canadian.
