I think all hon. members will realize the significance of this matter.
In this house we have possibly a special problem. We are a house which represents a bilingual country. We have no rules or regulations in this regard. We have in the past given approval to associations being incorporated and there has been no request for a translation. An official name has been requested. It is not customary to ask for a translation. I think hon. members realize that if it were possible to accept the translation of the short English phrase it would satisfy the proper function of this group which has been in existence and has done such wonderful work throughout the years. We would thereby protect any similar group of Canadians having the same endeavours in mind, and in that way there would be the recognition of the bilingual factor which we recognize is very special to Canada.
I make these remarks with the greatest frankness and with the desire to create the greatest possible harmony. There is no doubt that the Scouts of Canada, Scouts du Canada, by whatever name we may call them, will promote in Canada all these wonderful things which the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) mentioned to the house.
I should like to put this statement on the record. If the bill is read the second time and is referred to the committee which studies these private bills, I should want to make sure that all hon. members were informed of the situation, especially if the house felt it should grant the total application, that is to say the English name and the French name which is slightly different. If it granted both-something which is not usual in incorporations under the statutes of Canada-and a similar association later applied for a like name, possibly with the French appellation, hon. members would recall the debate today so that the association in the future would not be deprived of a right that we must agree it has, as have all other associations.

Private Bills

maintopic: THE CANADIAN GENERAL COUNCIL OF THE BOY SCOUTS ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 23, 1959, I had the privilege of introducing Bill No. S-13 on behalf of the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke (Mr. Fleming) concerning the holdings of real estate by the Boy Scouts Association.
This bill is comparatively simple. We have only a few minutes in which to deal with this matter, but I should like to point out two significant factors in it. The change of name includes the saving clauses which would prevent any legal difficulties in connection with such a change. The most obvious matter is that the name is short and made less difficult than the former nomenclature, namely the Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association. Shortening it up to "the Boy Scouts of Canada" will facilitate easy use of the name and it will be designated in such a way that it will be well known to all Canadians.
The second significant fact is that the new name removes any suggestion that the Canadian association is a branch or subsidiary of the British association. We know that in 1914 scouting was permitted by numerous provincial councils, but in June of that year the Canadian general council, with headquarters at Ottawa, was incorporated. That is the name under which the association has gone until the present time.
The present change to simply "Boy Scouts of Canada" will complete that change-over and will make it quite clear that the Canadian association is an autonomous unit in the boy scouts organizations of the world.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker):
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, supplementary protocol No. 1 to the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, supplementary protocol No. 2 to the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, and the memorandum of understanding on the application of article XV of the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development, all of which were signed in Paris on December 14, 1960; and that this house do approve the above agreements.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was discussing how I thought the organization for economic co-operation and development, the convention establishing which we are being asked to approve, could operate so as if not to ensure, at least to assist in ensuring that the European movement toward economic consolidation should take the right course; that consolidation and unity should not result in the raising of barriers against countries outside either the European free trade area or, more importantly, the European common market.
There have been worries and indeed some indications of danger on that score from the two sources which I mentioned, namely the averaging method used in setting the common market tariff against non-member

Economic Co-operation and Development
countries and the range of commodities for which duties established by the common market are fixed by negotiation.
In the first case, fears have been expressed -and perhaps there is some ground for them -that the increase in the German and Benelux tariffs that resulted from this averaging method will hurt outside countries more than the reduction in the French and Italian rates will help them by the application of the same averaging method.
It is true as the minister and hon. members will know, that the first 10 per cent cut inside the common market on internal tariffs on the way to completely removing these tariffs over the years was applied, I think without conditions, to the GATT countries, but the second 10 per cent cut which I believe took place in July of 1960-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-was not so extended although members of the common market could voluntarily extend that 10 per cent cut if they so desired. I think that the Netherlands is the only country that has done so.
It is now fairly clear, in my opinion, that if there is to be a further reduction of that kind it is to be extended to countries like Canada and the United States, GATT countries outside the common market only, if they will take reciprocal action in reducing their tariff toward common market countries. There is therefore a problem here which perhaps the O.E.C.D. will be able to take into consideration when it begins operation.
The second danger, namely the fixing by negotiation of duties for certain commodities, presents another problem. The duties in this respect include those on some commodities of great importance to Canada, such as basic raw and industrial materials. They are fixed at such levels that production within the common market may well develop with a consequent diversion of purchases from outside to inside suppliers. We have fears on this score particularly in connection with agricultural products.
The executive secretary of GATT in dealing with this subject has expressed the view that suppliers outside the common market will probably have a decreasing share of this market for agricultural commodities. That forecast was made presumably on plans to fix minimum prices for such products within the community regardless of conditions on the world markets and to protect these minimum prices by levies, quotas, controls and all that sort of thing.
No doubt it is considerations of this kind which are responsible for some of the fears I have expressed and which are being expressed in Canada. I believe it would be helpful indeed if the government would give
its own indication of the validity and importance of these fears and tell us what might be the effect on our exports. An appraisal of this kind given before this resolution is passed would be of assistance.
Before I leave that point, in turning to the more encouraging side I want to place on record a statement made by the president of the commission of the European economic community, Walter Hallstein, who said:
Not only must we continue, and perhaps increase, our present rate of economic growth. Not only must we prove that a free society is competitive. We must also help to stabilize and enlarge the markets we provide for the world's producers of raw materials, and, as the developing countries achieve greater industrial production, so we must develop, with them and accept from them, increasing quantities of manufactures.
The common market should develop along those lines. We would then have little to fear and much to hope from that kind of development.
Perhaps I could also say a word on the organization of the European free trade area and its possible effect on Canada. This free trade area, as we know, includes the United Kingdom. I am glad to say that an increasing percentage of our exports is now going to that market. Most of our exports to the United Kingdom, as part of the European free trade area, which lately have proved so important to us, will not be affected by any proposed arrangements inside the free trade area but there are other important exports which will meet increasing competition in the United Kingdom market as a result of the development of this free trade area.
This situation would be unfortunate at a time when we are doing everything we can to increase our exports to that market which has not only a value in itself but has-I was going to call it an incidental value, though it is more than that-the additional value of making us less dependent on the United States market.
We can all take satisfaction in the fact that our exports to the United Kingdom have increased. They have gone ahead during 1960. Whether we are able to continue this increase in our exports to the United Kingdom will depend on two things. It will depend in part on our willingness to import from them and not to put obstructions in the way of British exports to this country. It will also depend on the ability of the United Kingdom to buy anywhere because of growing exchange difficulties in that country. Although we hope this will not happen, those difficulties may interfere with our continued increase of sales in that market.
Great Britain's trade surplus is declining at the present time. In 1958 it was 800 million, in 1959 it was 140 million and in 1960

Economic Co-operation and Development it was estimated at only 50 million. To correct that situation which is causing a good deal of anxiety in the United Kingdom there are indications not only that the U.K. may have to take some kind of action against Canadian and other dollar imports. I hope it will not be done by reimposition of any of the controls from which we have been happily free in the last year or two. Rather I hope that- and this is equally important to Canada-the United Kingdom may feel impelled to move into the orbit of the common market. Certainly the information that one gets from the press is that the association of the United Kingdom with the common market is now being more closely considered than before. I know there are difficulties in regard to the United Kingdom coming into the common market; they are mainly difficulties arising out of agricultural trade, but there are ways by which those difficulties could be overcome. If they are overcome, and if the United Kingdom does move across the channel into this market, we would have to be careful indeed of the effect of this on our own interests.
Only this morning, as reported in the New York Times, the Lord Privy Seal of the United Kingdom, Mr. Edward Heath, made a statement as follows:
Edward Heath, Lord Privy Seal, Informed the six common market governments-
Presumably this would be yesterday.
-that Britain was willing to accept a common or "harmonized" external tariff on non-farm goods as part of a settlement.
That had been the key demand of the common market. Mr. Heath went on to say -and these words have a great significance for our country-that this, according to the press, was a fundamental change of principle in the United Kingdom position.
It would be interesting indeed to hear from the government whether they have any comment to make on what a member of the British cabinet called a fundamental change in the British position in respect of association with the common market.
I should like to put a little more of this report on the record because it is of such great significance. The report in the New York Times goes on to say:
Mr. Heath's proposal excluded agriculture. It also apparently left intact the present system of preferential tariffs for goods imported into Britain from the British commonwealth. However, Mr. Heath said Britain would have no objection to a reduction of the preferences her exports enjoy in commonwealth markets if the Six wanted to start negotiations with the commonwealth toward that end.
I cannot imagine anything much more important than that development announced only within the last few days, in British policy toward the common market. There was

no reference to this matter by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance but it would be interesting to get their comments on it.
It was not long ago that the Minister of Finance expressed great doubt indeed about the United Kingdom association with the common market, and he made some observations which have been interpreted as taking a strong position in regard to any move on the part of the United Kingdom for closer economic ties with the common market. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that a member of the British cabinet has now indicated that those closer ties are about to be negotiated.
Last November, at Ste. Adele, the Minister of Finance had this to say:
It is difficult for us to see how any accommodation which the United Kingdom might make with the Six could fail to damage to some degree, and perhaps seriously, Canadian interests.
Well, these negotiations are now taking place. The minister went on to say:
The ability of the Canadian government to maintain existing preferences in the Canadian market in favour of the United Kingdom would inevitably be affected by changes in the access of Canadian goods to the United Kingdom.
This development, which will undoubtedly have significance with respect to the organization about which we are talking about, can be one of great hope, and it can be one of danger to Canada. In my opinion, it involves- and I do not think I am using too strong words when I say this-a challenge to Canada's international economic policies. It seems to me there are four quite distinct lines of approach which a Canadian government could follow in meeting this situation. The first way would be to move in the direction of economic self-sufficiency through increased protectionism. The second way would be to move in the direction of economic integration with the United States. The third way would be to rely on GATT as the foundation of our trade policy and hope to achieve multilateralism in trade through further rounds of tariff negotiations. One of those rounds is under way now, I believe, in Geneva. The fourth way-and the one I think is the best way-is to move toward closer co-operation with Europe with the establishment of an Atlantic freer trade area as a long term goal of Canadian international economic policy to be achieved stage by stage.
So far as alternative one is concerned- and there is some indication that this is the government's preferred way, namely making ourselves economically more self-sufficient, moving toward economic nationalism-that way may provide a tempting short run answer to our difficulties. It may be the way, equally tempting, to Washington; but the experience of the 1930's showed that this

approach is sterile and self-defeating. You get indications of this approach in Washington at the present time in the hearings that are now being held there in regard to the approval of the very organization that we are being asked to approve in this House of Commons, where there is developing very strong opposition, no doubt fomented by certain pressure groups, against the ratification of this very convention.
The second alternative I mentioned was economic integration with the United States. We saw press reports of a proposal made not long ago in Toronto by a former member of the administration in Washington, namely Mr. McElroy, who put this proposal forward as a very responsible and serious way out of our economic difficulties. He put forward what he called a North American common market. The United States today is our most important single customer, of course. But the political and other kinds of anxiety caused by our economic relations with that country are more likely to be intensified than to be weakened and removed through seeking this solution of our increased difficulty with that country alone. That does not mean, of course, that we should eliminate the possibility of the closest possible trade relations with the United States as part of a wider Atlantic association. Indeed, our dependence on the United States would be lessened rather than increased if we could fashion a newer and wider economic association on an Atlantic basis of which the United States would become an indispensable part. While there may be in Washington influences which are leading in the opposite direction on the way to greater economic self-sufficiency, there are also in this new administration in Washington forces which I hope and believe are moving in the direction toward Atlantic coordination and freer trade within the Atlantic area.
The third alternative, Mr. Speaker, is reliance on GATT. Of course we ought to take full advantage of any further opportunities we have in Geneva for GATT negotiations and for accomplishing further reductions in tariff. I would be the first to agree that GATT has accomplished a great deal over the years in establishing the rule of law in trading relations, in making tariff increases difficult of achievement and in bringing about more extremely important general tariff decreases. During the post-war period GATT has undoubtedly been the chief instrument in tariff reduction and the liberalization of trade, but the question now arises whether GATT can make much further progress in this direction. In my view, and this will be shown in the negotiations at Geneva within the next weeks and months, a new approach
Economic Co-operation and Development outside GATT, by GATT countries in the Atlantic area, if you like, is required under the present circumstances. A new impetus, approach, or initiative should be taken and that new approach can best be taken by the Atlantic countries.
That brings me to the fourth possibility which I mentioned and which I think is the best possibility, namely that of working toward closer economic association between Europe on the one hand and North America on the other, which should take expression in the freeing of trade to the greatest possible extent stage by stage and steadily over the years on an Atlantic basis. That, Mr. Speaker, is not only the challenge but the hope of the future in international economic policy and I do not think that anything less than that will meet the challenge we face.
I express in this house the hope that the government will use its influence in the organization for economic co-operation and development in order to achieve this particular objective. O.E.C.D. could be the beginning of a new trade grouping to embrace the European economic community, the European free trade area, the United States, Canada and, through special arrangements, other free world countries which would like to join in the association. After all, if the European economic community can make arrangements with respect to countries outside that community in order to bring them in, so also could an enlarged Atlantic free trade area be able to make arrangements with countries outside the area so it would not develop in a discriminatory way, which is something, of course, that should be avoided.
That possibility, and it is a stimulating and exciting one, of something to be achieved in the long run, has, it seems to me, occurred to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) only to be quickly rejected by him because in his speech at Ste. Adele last November he had this to say:
When O.E.C.D. is established it will assume the functions of the trade committee. However, this should not be taken to mean that O.E.C.D. represents an accommodation between the North American and European countries, in an arrangement which will discriminate against the rest of the world. On the contrary, the core of the new body's activity will be consultation and discussion of general economic policies within the framework of the GATT and the international monetary fund.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can go further than that in O.E.C.D. and I hope we will do so. In contrast to that very cautious and limited view taken by the minister on that occasion, let me quote what the minister of trade and industry of West Germany had to say on this point of the extension of the European economic community to include Atlantic
2514	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Last November Dr. Erhard was interviewed by Bruce Hutchison and he was asked this question by Mr. Hutchison:
Do you believe the methods of the common market could be extended to include North America in an Atlantic free trade area?
Dr. Erhard's answer was: "In principle, yes". He went on to say that it would have to be brought about in two stages, that first you would have to bring in the European free trade area, including the United Kingdom, and some progress is being made in that direction, and then afterwards North America. He went on to say that Germany would help to make this possible by agreeing to special arrangements to cover commonwealth preferences, which he admitted are a difficulty. He said he believed that it was not only desirable but absolutely necessary for Great Britain to join the European common market. Then he used these words which I think are the heart of the matter:
It is not a question of finding technical solutions but a political will.
Europe cannot develop toward unity alone. He ended by saying:
It will be sufficiently strong only within the framework of the Atlantic community.
We on this side, Mr. Speaker, have been advocating consideration of an Atlantic free trade area since the fall of 1957 as a result of important changes which occurred in the world before and after that time. In our view that is the only kind of international economic association which will not only meet the challenge of our own necessity for expanding production and trade but will also meet the economic challenge of the communist bloc.
We have not had much support for that view in the house. It was only a few days ago that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) in Montreal jeered at the idea of an Atlantic free trade area in which Canada would be a member. But this, Mr. Speaker, must be the objective toward which we work in the present circumstances. When we put forward this idea it has been laughed at as imaginary, idealistic and unrealistic just as the European common market was regarded ten years ago, but nevertheless some distinguished advocates have come out in support of it. I refer to Mr. Adlai Stevenson, governor Rockefeller, Mr. Erhard whom I have mentioned, the prime minister of Denmark and many other western leaders who have come to the same view. In Canada the Canadian Labour Congress and farm organizations now support the idea of expanding trade on an Atlantic basis.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, Canada has a wonderful opportunity to take the lead in initiating and pushing this idea in this new organization


that we will hope to support when the discussion on this resolution is completed. Canada can take a leading part in this organization in the direction I have just outlined. Because the words are more fitting than any I could find to support this idea, perhaps I might quote Mr. Bruce Hutchison in an article on this subject on December 14, 1960, in which he had this to say:
The lesson of these events-
He is referring to the development of the European economic community and the European free trade area.
-is perfectly clear. Somehow, without any narrow, doctrinaire logic but with flexible, pragmatic methods and by reasonable stages, the principles that made the European six the most prosperous area of the free world must be spread through the whole North Atlantic community and beyond.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow a question? A moment ago he picked up a slip of paper which apparently had on it a statement to which he made reference. The statement was that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had jeered at any proposal for an Atlantic trading arrangement. I wonder whether the hon. member has that slip of paper because I should like to know to what he made reference.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
I was referring to a report in the Montreal Star of a meeting in Montreal on February 13, about which there was also a report on the radio. It was tc the effect that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had criticized a top Liberal spokesman-that was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)-for advocating an Atlantic free trade area recently and had said that such an agreement would result in the shutting down of many Canadian factories and mass unemployment. On the radio report there was a good deal of additional detail as to the minister's attitude and what the minister had said, that if we kept pushing this visionary scheme of an Atlantic free trade area we would put people out of work in Canada at the present time and that would be a fine way of curing unemployment. I think that is not an unfair paraphrase of the attitude of the minister.
Of course, the answer to that is simply that this is the kind of thing that will have to be done stage by stage, as I have emphasized, over the years. The same thing could have been said about the European common market ten years ago, namely that if the European countries come together, if they abolish tariffs between them as they are doing, they will put people out of work in their own country. Instead of that happening, they have proceeded stage by stage in the reduction and eventual elimination of tariffs and in the last

two years they have made that area the most prosperous trading area in the world. I suggest the same technique, based on the same principle and applied over the wider Atlantic area might, over the years, have an equally desirable result. This is the time, of all times, when we need that result both nationally and internationally.
This is what Mr. Hutchison said, Mr. Speaker, in one of his articles on this matter and I should like to subscribe to this statement:
If the process of regional splintering goes on, and the splinters, when formed, restrict one another's trade, then Canada will find itself ground between them.
Our national identity in the end will only be safe within the widest possible grouping of free nations trading abundantly.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
The resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), Mr. Speaker, asking parliament to ratify the organization for economic cooperation and development is undoubtedly an important one and I am sure that it will receive the approval of the members of this house. This organization, as members are well aware, is composed of some 20 countries that will come together under the rules set out in this document to consult and to consider ways and means of improving trading relations, improving the national economy and providing aid to underdeveloped countries.
The purposes of the organization are set forth in part in article 1 as follows:
The aims of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (hereinafter called the "Organization") shall be to promote policies designed:
(a)	to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability, and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy;
I feel that the impetus for this kind of organization has come largely from the success of the countries involved in O.E.E.C. and the common market. They have shown, by consultation and by common programs, that they have been able to raise their standards of living substantially. The fact of the matter is that their standards of living have gone up at a great rate, so successful have they been in arranging their economic affairs. It has been the lack of growth of the countries on the North American continent that have given the impetus to the development of this kind of organization for consultation and for the drawing up of plans.
The O.E.E.C. has been successful in that the countries comprising this organization have made a marvellous recovery in recent years. I am quoting now from an article in the 90205-6-160
Economic Co-operation and Development Regina Leader-Post of October 8, 1960 in which is set forth some of the accomplishments of O.E.E.C.:
As an indication of the growth of O.E.E.C. countries during the 1948-58 period their gross national production has risen 62 per cent, industrial production, 95 per cent, volume of imports from the rest of the world, 56 per cent, volume of exports to the countries of the world 130 per cent, volume of intra-European trade 183 per cent, and population has risen 9 per cent.
There are new developments in Europe today such as the common market and the outer seven. These developments not only show great promise for the countries involved but they pose certain definite dangers for the Canadian economy. I am certain that this kind of organization in which Canada can consult with other member nations can be helpful in working out arrangements so that the welfare of our own nation may be better assured in the years to come. The nations involved in O.E.C.D. comprise not only the nations that belong to NATO but certain additional nations. Over the years many of us have hoped that under article 2 of the NATO treaty economic co-operation and economic arrangements within the NATO organization would be achieved. This development would help the member nations in an economic way. Article 2 has largely been a failure. Economic co-operation has not been forthcoming. NATO has become more and more a military organization and little else.
As a result of the failure of NATO to take advantage of article 2, the organization now under discussion has been made necessary. If O.E.C.D. is a success, as all of us hope it will be, then the more certainty there is that in the years ahead NATO will be a military organization and article 2 will continue to be a part of the treaty that is not being used. I can see definite advantages in the development of O.E.C.D. rather than the development of article 2 under NATO. Nations are coming into O.E.C.D. that are not attached to NATO. It has been said that such countries as Yugoslavia and Finland are showing an interest in O.E.C.D. They wish to become connected with this organization, either in the capacity of observers or associate members.
I feel that such an organization is much more likely to make a contribution to the peaceful relations of the world than would be possible under NATO. I think O.E.C.D., in the provision of economic aid to member nations or to nations outside of the organization, is much more likely to be successful than is the NATO organization in the provision of this economic aid. After all, the underdeveloped countries of Africa and Asia have felt that NATO was a strictly military organization and to accept any assistance from this organization would make them a part of the

Economic Co-operation and Development cold war struggle. These nations, in our opinion, are much more likely to accept aid from O.E.C.D. We feel, therefore, that this is another reason why this organization deserves the support of all members of this house.
I feel that we should be making a mistake if we believed that the establishment of this organization would correct some of the great trading problems that face this nation or correct some of our own internal economic problems. After all, this organization is just a consultative organization. There are no economic agreements flowing from this organization. Within this organization there is no plan for more trade or for the solving of unemployment. There is merely at this time machinery for consultation and the establishment or continuation of a large number of committees that will look into various economic questions. Mr. Speaker, I think we should be all the more interested in the purposes of this organization because it sets as one of its purposes the maintenance of a high level of employment. Certainly Canada needs a high level of employment at this time.
Perhaps through this organization the government can learn ways and means of dealing with the economic problems that face our nation both internally and in the field of international trade. I do not believe there is in the present constitution any provision for a consultative assembly or for a parliamentary organization. I think a consultative assembly or a parliamentary organization would be a useful addition to the committees that are established under this treaty. I would hope that in the days ahead as the organization unfolds and develops there may be a consultative assembly to which parliamentary representation may be made.
We are greatly interested in the effect of the common market on Canada. We are interested in finding out if we can the Canadian government's policy in relation to the common market. We were disturbed when, the government of the United Kingdom having offered to Canada the possibility of establishing a free trade area, our government shied away and refused to come forward with any policy as far as the development of a free trade with the United Kingdom was concerned. The common market poses a threat to Canada. The nations in the common market have been taking, over the years, some 30 per cent of Canadian exports. Our markets for these exports on the common market are not assured and there seems to be every possibility that the United Kingdom in the days ahead might join the common market. If this should happen it will

pose a very serious threat to Canadian exports and to our Canadian economy.
At this time the development of widespread consultation among the nations of the Atlantic community is necessary. We think this organization can play a useful role. We look forward to the reduction of trade barriers in this larger group of nations. We think that the destiny of Canada depends to a large extent on the expansion of trade, and the expansion of exports to the various nations of the world. We believe that within this organization we can expect that there will be an improvement in trade relations among the nations concerned. We welcome the resolution and we shall lend our support to the establishment of this organization. We do point out that it is merely a consultative organization and that for the development of the Canadian economy our government must develop new and concrete policies, to which this organization at this time will be of very little help.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution requires parliament to ratify an agreement which will bring into existence a new organization to be known as the organization for economic co-operation and development. This new organization will replace a somewhat similar organization which was established I believe in 1948. As you look over the membership of this organization you will find that probably the main difference between the new organization and the old one, which was known as the organization for economic co-operation, is that the organization which will be set up in consequence of this resolution will consist of 20 members instead of 18. The two new members that will be added are Canada and the United States.
The aims of this new organization are highly commendable. They are set forth in article 1 as follows:
(a)	to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability, and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy;
(b)	to contribute to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development;
(c)	to contribute to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations.
These are worthy and challenging objectives but whether they will be attained or not will, in my opinion, depend on the willingness of the member countries to commit themselves to a greater measure of co-operation and even sacrifice than has been evident in the past. If we look at those membership countries we find that 13 soon found it necessary to form smaller groups outside

the main organization. We have six of them banded together in what is known as the European common market or the inner six. Seven more of them are banded together in the European free trade association-

-commonly referred to as the outer seven. The fact that this large group of nations had to break up into smaller groups is, I think, evidence that they were unable to solve their most pressing problems as members of that larger group.
As we look back over the history of trading groups the prospects are, in my opinion, not too optimistic.

speechtext:
My hon. and juvenile friend is entitled to his little joke and I should not wish to interfere with his fun at this moment. However, this is a rather serious topic and I am trying to deal with it in a serious manner.
Hon. members will remember that not very long ago the government of Canada was criticized for adhering too rigidly to what is known as GATT. As has already been pointed out this evening, GATT obtained a good many benefits for its member nations but it fell far short of what was expected of it. It fell far short of expectations because it contained a good many loopholes and too many member countries were willing to take advantage of the escape hatches.
We can also think back to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. There were hopes that once NATO had completed its organization to deal with immediate defence problems it would then develop into a trading community. That hope also has been dashed. If we wish to come nearer home I suppose we only have to think back to NORAD, because I do not think any member of this house will assert that, as far as sharing of defence production is concerned, the NORAD agreement has fulfilled our expectations. Therefore I can assure the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) that history is not too reassuring on this particular point.
These high hopes we had in the case of GATT, NATO and NORAD have foundered, and they have all foundered on the rock of self-interest. If this new organization which we are discussing today is not to meet the same fate, we must find a purpose greater 90205-6-160J
Economic Co-operation and Development than self-interest on which every member country can unite and to which every member country can commit itself.
This afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said it was his hope that through this organization member countries would make a full contribution to a world community. I am sure we all share that hope, but let us not deceive ourselves that this objective is going to be accomplished merely by setting up another organization. If there is any comment to be made I think it should be that perhaps we have too many organizations overlapping and all trying to do the same job. Perhaps it is a case of too many cooks spoiling the broth.
Let us not forget this point. If this organization is to fulfil our hopes in making the fullest contribution to a world community, in the final analysis the matter boils down to individuals. First of all it boils down to the people who are responsible for the industry and commerce of the member countries. Many of the nations included in this membership, particularly Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, west Germany and others are countries which are pledged, at least politically, to a system of free enterprise. It means that those who are responsible for the workings of free enterprise in our country and in other countries must themselves find a purpose greater than self-interest.
Free enterprise has a great many good points. It has developed mass-production techniques. It has produced a quantity of cheap goods and made them available on a wide scale to many people at reasonable prices. It has encouraged a spirit of adventure and the development of genius and invention. These things are all good, but let us not forget that free enterprise also has its faults. While it has accomplished much, it has also led to labour troubles, to bitterness, to class war, and in many cases to a misuse of materials and of natural wealth.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also intend to support the resolution now before the house. However, I should like to make some brief observations in this respect.
I agree with the statement made by my leader to the effect that this new organization for economic co-operation and development will in effect replace article 2 of NATO.
In this house and the other place we have an organization known as the Canadian NATO parliamentarians' association. I believe it would be proper if that association would reconstitute itself in order to be known as the Canadian NATO parliamentarians' association in support of the aims and ideals of O.E.C.D. because the association was originally organized to lend support to the implementation of article 2 of NATO. That association ought now to be reconstituted as an association in support of the furtherance of the aims of O.E.C.D. However, my main reason for rising is that I have given considerable thought to article 1 of the convention. Article 1 lists the aims of the organization for economic co-operation and development. Aim (a) reads:
To achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability, and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy.
It is my contention that at the same time as we are being asked to subscribe to this convention our government stands guilty of a violation of the very first aim listed in the convention, because no one can claim-and I do not think the government would do so- that we have reached anywhere near the highest sustainable economic growth in our nation. We are simply marking time in our national productivity. Canadian agriculture is even being advised to produce less. Canadian industrialists are working not around the clock but on short weeks. They are locking up their plants for as long as one month, ostensibly for purposes of retooling. Many of our industries are locked up completely. If, as the convention says, Canada is to contribute to the development of the world economy, we certainly will be unable to do so if we continue to insist that we can afford
2520	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Economic Co-operation and Development to have over halt a million unemployed in our country and if we can have Canadian agriculture producing at a rate much below its capabilities.
I find it a little hard to agree to a convention when I realize that we are violating the very first aim listed. Let us look at the next aim listed. We are pledged:
To contribute to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development.
We note, as do many Canadians, with regret that our government is reducing its annual contribution to the development of the underdeveloped areas of the world. I believe our contribution this year is less than it was last year by a number of millions of dollars, and we certainly are guilty of not obeying the spirit of this aim either.
Under the last aim listed in article 1 we pledge ourselves:
To contribute to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has before the house a resolution which will in effect increase Canadian tariffs on imported goods. How that ties in with asking us in the same week to subscribe to a convention in which we pledged ourselves to make our contribution to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral basis is difficult indeed for me to understand. In one item of legislation we are asked to increase tariffs. In the next item of legislation we are asked to give our pledge that we will encourage expansion of world trade on a multilateral basis.
May I return for only a moment to our pledge under aim (b). I have a return which was supplied to me in the House of Commons on November 23 last. I asked this question:
As of December 31, 1959, what was the estimated extent of foreign investment in Canada, and what was the estimated extent of Canadian investment outside of Canada?
The answer I received reads as follows:
As of December 31, 1959, the value of foreign long term investments in Canada is estimated at $20.7 billion and the value of Canadian long term capital investments outside of Canada is estimated at $5.5 billion.
We are importers of capital at a time when we are pledging ourselves to do what we can to make investment capital available in greater amounts to other nations of the world.
I have also a list, in a reply I received on the same day, of our contributions abroad, and it states that in 1959 the federal government gifts abroad totalled $71 million and federal government loans abroad totalled $1.4 million, apart from an increase in Canada's quota in the international monetary fund involving payments of $239 million including $177 million in notes.
[Mr. Regier.l
I notice in the annual report of the international development bank that for every $1 that Canada has invested in the international development bank, as a result of that investment $2 was spent in Canada for the purchase of Canadian goods. If we want to make our economy move, international aid is one way of doing it; it is one way of making our economy healthy and causing it to move ahead. This money is not lost to us; it is not lost to our economy. The supplying of international aid creates employment for Canadians here in making the capital goods that the underdeveloped nations of the world need.
I notice that for every $1 invested by the United Kingdom in the international development bank, $3 worth of goods were purchased in the United Kingdom in connection with the project for which the invested money was used. It is therefore good business, and an aid to our economy, for us greatly to enhance our overseas assistance. I hope the day is not far distant when Canada will meet the recommendations of the United Nations in this respect and that we shall decide to aid underdeveloped nations at least to the extent of one per cent of our gross national production. At the present time our rate is less than one fifth of one per cent and yet we are potentially the richest people on earth and our standard of living takes second place only to that of the United States. In gifts abroad we ought to be spending, or we ought to have spent in 1959 a minimum of $345 million rather than $71 million. That would have been one per cent of our gross national product.
As I said before, I regret to note that this year the government is planning on doing even less than it has been doing in the last number of years, and that the estimates have been reduced in this regard. Therefore, I feel that when we are asked to subscribe to a convention which lists aims (a), (b) and (c) we ought not to have to admit to ourselves that we stand already in violation of these three aims. If we are going to have unemployment, if we are going to have curtailed production, we will not have the wealth that is necessary for us to make our proper contribution on the world scene today. In addition, if we are going to raise our tariffs we ought not to pledge that we are going to support increased multilateral trade among the nations.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the matter which he has presented to the house today, is one that possesses at least a great potential importance. If the expectations for

the new organization embraced in the convention which we are asked to adopt, should be realized, it could mean a great deal not only for the United States, Canada and the other 18 member states of the organization but also, from the point of view of an intensification in the political and economic unity of Europe and, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I would hope a much wider area covered by the phrase, an Atlantic freer trade grouping of nations.
But in supporting the resolution in its present form I think we must not make the mistake of attributing to it qualities that it does not possess. Undoubtedly many did expect and anticipate for this organization a greater flexibility in its provisions; and on that account a greater effectiveness in dealing with the problem it was designed to meet. That problem, as I see it, concerns the enabling of certain countries not members of the two existing European economic blocs to enjoy a liaison in the first place with those two blocs, and in the course of time to evolve an arrangement which will permit the nonparticipating nations to enjoy satisfactory trading relations with the common market and with the European free trade association.
Undoubtedly what Mr. Dillon had in mind a year and a half ago was to provide through O.E.C.D. a nexus or a liaison between the common market in particular and the United States and Canada. To the extent that his efforts have succeeded I think we owe him a great debt for the successful negotiations which may largely be attributed to his efforts. These negotiations began when he was under secretary of state and were achieved when he became secretary of the treasury in the government of the United States.
I think, however, in order to understand fully the merits and weaknesses of the convention, as it is now presented, one must look at the Canadian scene. Certainly if we are to judge it at all, we must judge the convention first of all in terms of our own interests and then, of course, in terms of its effectiveness in meeting a problem that engulfs all the free nations at this critical time in the history of the world. The fact is that very real dangers do exist under present world trading arrangements. If we in Canada are to avoid these dangers it is absolutely essential that our policies be clearly outlined for all the world to see.
I think we may well ask the government today, what is Canadian policy in this regard at the present time? Are we consciously moving toward greater protectionism with the intention presumably of becoming economically self-sufficient or more economically selfsufficient? Are we still in favour of a freer multilateral trading world or are our policies
Economic Co-operation and Development directed toward closer economic integration with the United States? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in the public pronouncements he has made from time to time has given us reason to believe that government policy with regard to the responses to these three questions is ambiguous. I have before me a statement made by a distinguished and intelligent Canadian businessman who has expressed his concern in this regard. I refer to Mr. R. H. Fowler of Montreal who said:
It is difficult to discover, except in most general terms, what Canada's attitude is toward the common market and the outer seven trading blocs in Europe. I suggest that, wherever you turn in this field, there is uncertainty and vagueness both in official Canadian policy and in private industrial attitudes on trading questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext: What was the date?

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
This was last fall. I continue:
Whatever the democratic processes are that should operate to develop national trading policies, they do not seem to be working very effectively in Canada at the moment.
This complaint of Mr. Fowler is not a single complaint. It is to be found not only in the positions taken by parties in this house but in the positions taken by businessmen and others throughout the country. One minute we are led to believe that the Minister of Finance is against the common market in Europe; and if we are to judge from the speech he made at Ste. Adele as reported by the Canadian press on November 18 there is no doubt that what he has said on some occasions in Canada is consistent with the attitude that he was reported as having taken toward the common market in his discussions with the chancellor of the exchequer a few months ago in the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext: That was a remarkable speech he made.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-APPROVAL OF CONVENTION AND RELATED AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
If we examine the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) about ten days ago in Montreal, we will find that he too, although he is Minister of Trade and Commerce, has his doubts about the common market, about a multilateral trading world, and about the desirability of removing economic discrimination, although we learn from the morning papers today that his deputy minister, in a speech delivered yesterday in Montreal, took the position that these things deserve our careful attention. Indeed, as I intend to show before I conclude, the deputy minister of trade and commerce regards the common market as both an opportunity and a challenge for Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, of course, notwithstanding the fact that he was one of the co-signatories to the
2522	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development convention on behalf of Canada, I believe, looks upon these instruments, according to some of his pronouncements, as media that should not be encouraged by Canada.
Undoubtedly the common market does hold dangers for Canada in terms of some of its trading aspects. Certain of our goods undoubtedly will suffer in the short term. In the long term certain of our products will stand to obtain an advantage. But this much is clear. Having in mind the problems that beset the western world at the present time, involving conflict with the tremendous economic drive that the Soviet union and its satellite powers are making, we cannot help but encourage any effort that seeks to bring about the unification of Europe, something that we have been striving for in the western world since the end of the first world war, and which Mr. Churchill himself said was an essential element in the foundation not only of European unity but also of world peace.
A few moments ago I put forward some questions with regard to Canadian policy at the present time. I suggested that the answers to three questions are varied, depending upon which speech is made by which minister in which month and on which occasion in which country. The fact is that before we can have a clear policy we must have certain objectives. I suggest to the house that there are three broad objectives which Canada must pursue if we are to meet our challenges in this shrinking world. We must have economic growth and stability in Canada, unfettered by the threat of economic domination from the United States or, for that matter, from any country. We must assist other countries of the free world in achieving economic growth and stability in order that we may meet the east-west challenge. We must do everything within our power to assist the underdeveloped nations of the world to raise their economic development under freedom in order to meet the north-south challenge.
Undoubtedly, the greatest threat to our trading interests is the growing trend toward regionalism, whether it be in Europe or Latin America or even the attempts at certain regionalism right on the North American continent itself. But be that as it may, we cannot overlook the fact that certain developments of the greatest consequence have taken place in Europe. I refer to the Six and the Seven. We cannot stand still in these currents, no matter what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) may say or may have said. I feel that the direction in which we should be proceeding is clear. We in North America must work to associate ourselves with the unity of Europe, and not only with the unity


of Europe but with the unity of nations that are like-minded and are prepared to share in the building of that unity.
This is what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had in mind today. This is what he had in mind when, on other occasions, he has spoken about the desirability of expanding the unity that now exists in such blocs as the common market to take in other Atlantic countries and even to go beyond that, by embracing countries like Australia, New Zealand, Japan or any other country that is prepared to recognize the essential requirement for economic and political peace at this time, through multilateral trade arrangements. When the Leader of the Opposition spoke on this theme last March he concluded what he had to say by observing, "One thing is certain: If we want to become more independent and less dependent, then we must become more interdependent."
I am not so naive as to fail to recognize that there are difficulties in building such an area as an Atlantic free trade area. This is not the same thing as the common market. This is not the same thing which Mr. McElroy, the former secretary of defence in the United States, proposed in Toronto a short time ago when he proposed a common market between Canada and the United States. I am not talking about that matter, and that is not what the Leader of the Opposition was talking about. That is a special arrangement that would have to be examined with the greatest care, having in mind the interests of all parts of the two countries concerned. But if we are going to take into account the implications of the cold war now, we must recognize that if the free nations are to face increasingly severe economic competition from the Soviet bloc they must proceed along the lines suggested by the Leader of the Opposition today and on other occasions, both in this house and elsewhere.
The statement today by the Minister of Finance makes it apparent that there is not full agreement between what he had to say and what Mr. Dillon said, when the latter appeared before the Senate of the United States on February 14 last. This may result from the fact that Mr. Dillon was confronted with a particular problem in that country in connection with ratification, and found it necessary to give an emphasis which the Minister of Finance did not give today. It is only fair to say, however, that while I do find a different emphasis in the statements made by Mr. Dillon and the Minister of Finance, both are agreed on the threefold objective of O.E.C.D. They agree that it will be a major forum for efforts to harmonize financial and economic policies for the growth

and stability of most of the industrialized nations of the world whose economic behaviour significantly influences the course of the world economy and the trend of international payments. Second, it will provide a solid framework for intensive and frequent international consultation on the financial and monetary policies which must be pursued in order to achieve and maintain a better balance in the international payments position.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the main arguments the United States officials offered to congress with regard to this matter, because O.E.C.D. confers on the United States a better chance of maintaining a balance in the international payments position which confronts that country. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that that may well be one of the reasons, apart from the general reasons I have given why Canada should want to see this particular convention ratified early.
Third, the secretary of the treasury points out that O.E.C.D. will bring into being an organization of vital importance for assisting, on a co-operative basis, the development of the countries of the world. The last objective is an important one, because there are certain nations now, notably West Germany and Japan, which do not contribute to the underdeveloped countries anything like the extent which their own economies would justify and permit. The United States and Canada have been, I believe, relatively generous in the assistance they have provided bilaterally to the underdeveloped countries of the world through the Colombo plan. I do not for one moment say that there is not more that we could do. But other countries, likewise, have an obligation, particularly certain of the European nations, and that obligation is imposed on them not only in relation to the particular countries with whom they have had an historic commercial connection, but in relation to the underdeveloped countries of the world as well.
Is O.E.C.D. to completely replace the implications and the intentions originally provided under article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization? It is now a matter of record that the United States regards NATO as essentially a defensive organization. I share fully the view of the Leader of the Opposition that strong and continued support must be given to NATO in the critical situation that confronts us at this time. Instead of lessening our support for NATO in any way, we must make every effort to make NATO a stronger organization to meet the challenge presented. There can be no shirking of our responsibilities in NATO, but
Economic Co-operation and Development we in Canada believe that NATO would be a stronger organization if more attention had been paid to the directions of article 2 in that treaty and if there had been some recognition and some acknowledgement made by the United States, that one of the ways of building up a strong political defensive alliance was to recognize that all nations in that alliance had not only political but economic problems, economic objectives and economic concerns as well. It is suggested now, because of the sponsorship of O.E.C.D. by Mr. Dillon, that what the government of the United States really proposes is that whatever might have been done under article 2 of the NATO treaty might now be done under the new organization, namely O.E.C.D. It is suggested that NATO's economic role now is as dead as a dodo. That is the current opinion of some in Washington.
It would be well if we had from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) some assurance today in that regard. How does the United States look upon the O.E.C.D? Does it look upon it as a means of escaping the clear desirabilities in article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization? It may be that, because the new organization will cover a number of countries not in NATO, such as Ireland and Spain, the intention is to create a much wider constituency of interest, and to see that the aims originally intended to be covered are embraced by O.E.C.D. itself.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that the new organization is to have an executive, the secretary general, who many in this house know in the person of Mr. Kristensen, the former distinguished minister of finance in Denmark, and a former professor of one of that country's illustrious universities. I am sure the Minister of Finance was justified in saying that there is perhaps no man in this particular field better endowed and likely to be more dedicated to the prosecution of the objectives of O.E.C.D. But I think that we must take into account certain facts, and those facts are that the new body has no new executive and will have few fixed obligations. It will be less powerful than O.E.E.C. although I fully agree with the Minister of Finance that Canada and the United States have the right to participate much more directly in the new organization than they did in O.E.E.C.
However, one of the reasons that O.E.C.D. will be less powerful is the reluctance of France and the United States to co-ordinate their economic policies fully with other countries.
The minister said nothing about this matter in his statement today. He did not tell us that the agreement before us represents a compromise which, in the view of the United States government, would not compel the
2524	HOUSE OF
Economic Co-operation and Development government of that country to co-ordinate its actions with others except when it wanted to do so. That lack makes the organization at least in its present constituent terms less powerful and less effective than was the case when the full form and the full plan had been exposed to the world about a year and a half ago by Mr. Dillon himself.
One may join with other members, such as the one who has just spoken, in asking if we are now to ascertain from this new organization that there will be imposed on governments the aim to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in not only member countries but in one's own country. We have had no evidence from the government today of its determination to provide for an increase in the standard of living or to provide for a reduction in the unemployment which confronts our country in more serious proportions now than it does any one of the other 19 members of this organization. We have not heard a word about this matter from the Minister of Finance today. The Minister of Finance of course dodges this question continually. He has been dodging now for almost two and one quarter months. In his baby budget he made only one proposal which was designed to relieve unemployment. I refer to the provision for double depreciation in what he calls chronic unemployment areas and what I call depressed areas.
